ALAPUZHA CIRCLE, KUNNUMPURAM, ALAPUZHA-688 012.

R1-R2 BY SRI.RAMESH CHAND(PP)
OTHER PRESENT:

THIS CRIMINAL MISC. CASE HAVING COME UP FOR ADMISSION ON 06.02.2020, THE COURT ON THE SAME DAY PASSED THE FOLLOWING:
 Crl.M.C.No.7516 of 2019  2  O R D E R Dated this the 6th day of February 2020 The petitioners are aggrieved by their implication in S.T.No.32/2019 on the files of the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-II, Alappuzha, for having allegedly committed the offences punishable under Sections 3(zz)(v) & (vii) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (for short "the Act") read with Regulation 3.1.2(6) of the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards & Food Additives) Regulations, 2011 (for short "the Regulations").
2.

The specific allegation is that the 1st accused, who is the Officer-in-charge of the Resort, sold 2.00 kgs. of Moong Dal, which was kept in the premises, to the Food Safety Officer and the said Moong Dal was found contained a synthetic food colour, namely, Tartrazine, which according to Regulation 3.1.2(6) of the Regulations is not permissible and therefore the article is adulterated.
3. The petitioners contention are two fold.
The first contention is that Moong Dal is not meant for sale and therefore it was not sold or rather it was seized by the Food Safety Officer.
What is sold in a Resort is only articles prepared at the Restaurant and for the preparation of said articles the said additive, namely, Tartrazine, can be used.

The Food Safety Officer's contention is that the Moong Dal in its primary form cannot be mixed with an additive, namely, Tartrazine, and therefore it an additive, which is not permissible and it is not a prepared item, which contained Tartrazine.
4. The learned Counsel for the petitioners would contend that only when it is sold can the provisions under the Act is attracted.

But Section 38(1)(a)(ii) indicates that the Food Safety Officer may take a sample of any article of food or substance which is found by him on or in any such premises and therefore Moong Dal, which was purchased by him from the 1st accused can be held up for adulteration under the Act, in case it is found to be so.
5.
I find that since the Food Safety Officer has the authority to seize and collect samples of food articles kept in the premises, prima facie there is nothing wrong.

Whether the article was available for sale or whether it was actually sold or seized by the Food Safety Officer is a matter of evidence,
which can be decided by the trial court.

2 6.

sentences.text: The next argument raised by the learned Counsel for the petitioners is that petitioners 2 and 3 are the Managing Partner and Partner respectively of the 4th petitioner-Firm and therefore they do not have any direct connection with the alleged sale or seizure of the articles and therefore, they need to be exonerated.
The 1st petitioner is a person, who was conducting the business on behalf of the Firm and alleged to be directly responsible.
The 2nd petitioner is the Managing Partner of the 4th petitioner-Firm and therefore he also could be held to be responsible for the act of the 1st petitioner.
The extent of his liability is something to be determined by the trial court during the trial.

The 3rd petitioner is the wife of the 2nd petitioner and is only a Partner simpliciter and therefore under Section 66 of the Act it cannot be said that she has direct connection with the alleged act of selling Moong Dal to the Food Safety Officer and therefore the 3rd petitioner will have to be exonerated.

Under the above circumstances, the Crl.M.C. is allowed in part and the proceedings as against the 3 rd petitioner in S.T.No.32/2019 on the files of the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-II,
Alappuzha, stands quashed under Section 482, Cr.P.C.
